findings.why: 'Dark Spot Clearing' promises to clear spots, an elimination claim, while the body's 'visibly reduces dark spots' is the scoped version. Even as a product name it still reads as a claim.
findings.fix: Turmeric Face Serum that visibly reduces the appearance of dark spots

findings.span: Visibly Reduces Dark Spots from Day 7
findings.why: A result promised from day 7 needs a study of that duration with its qualifier on the ad; the body heading repeats it with no qualifier.
findings.fix: Visibly Reduces the Appearance of Dark Spots (keep 'from Day 7' only with its study footnote on the creative)

findings.span: clear from the very first week
findings.why: This is a second time-bound promise (radiant, glowing, clear skin within the first week) with no study qualifier; 'clear' next to 'acne spots' can also read as an acne-clearing claim.
findings.fix: Remove the timeframe: 'visibly diminishes the appearance of acne spots, sun spots and age spots'.

findings.why: 'Safe for all skin types' is a blanket safety promise that can't be substantiated for every user, least of all for a 10% glycolic acid serum; being tested doesn't make it safe for everyone.
findings.fix: Suitable for all skin types. Follow up with sunscreen.

findings.why: Leading with 'organically sourced' turmeric sells on naturalness, which Minimalist avoids; the brand leads with the active and its strength, and an organic claim also needs certification on file.

rule_hit_review.why: 'Clinically Tested' is an evidence claim; it needs the study on file and should say what was tested.
10% Glycolic Acid is stated identically in the headline and body and nothing attached contradicts it; the flag only reflects that this isn't a Minimalist strength. Confirm against the product label.
2% Niacinamide is stated consistently in the headline and body, and no product page contradicts it. Confirm against the label.
'Clinically tested face serum that visibly diminishes...' ties a clinical claim to results; it needs the study and its qualifier.
Second 'Clinically tested' claim; same substantiation needed.
'dermatologically tested' is an evidence claim (the rulebook's own fail example); it needs the test on file or narrower wording that says what was actually done.
Body repeat of '10% Glycolic Acid', consistent with the headline; no evidence of a mismatch. Confirm against the label.
Mis-paired match: the '2%' belongs to Niacinamide, not 'Acid', and it is consistent with the headline.

tone_read: Partly educational (it names 10% glycolic acid and 2% niacinamide and says what each does), but nearly every line repeats radiance mood words ('radiant, glowing') and an organic-turmeric story. The day-7 and first-week promises and the blanket 'safe' line are not Minimalist's understated register.
language_read: Concentrations are written in the brand's format (10%, 2%) and 'visibly reduces' is properly hedged, but 'Dark Spot Clearing' and 'Niacinamide reduces marks' are unscoped. 'Organically sourced' and 'cold pressed' turmeric is natural framing the brand doesn't use.
